title: The authority and urgency trick — question explanation
learningObjective: Recognize manipulation using urgency, authority or familiarity
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A caller says they are the principal’s assistant and demands your class portal password immediately because “the principal has approved it.”
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Recognize manipulation using urgency, authority or familiarity
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option D: Refuse to disclose the password and verify the request through an official contact channel. Authority pressure and urgency are common social-engineering cues; passwords should not be shared.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option A: Temporary disclosure still compromises the account and may enable immediate access. Option B: Claims of authority are easy to make and do not justify password disclosure. Option C: Knowing a name is not independent identity verification.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Refuse credential disclosure. End the interaction and confirm any legitimate request through a published contact channel. Authority, familiarity and urgency are persuasion techniques—not proof of identity.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.
scenes.onScreenText: Authority, familiarity and urgency are persuasion techniques—not proof of identity.

narration: Scenario: A caller says they are the principal’s assistant and demands your class portal password immediately because “the principal has approved it.” Safest response: Option D: Refuse to disclose the password and verify the request through an official contact channel. Authority pressure and urgency are common social-engineering cues; passwords should not be shared. Option A is unsafe because Temporary disclosure still compromises the account and may enable immediate access. Option B is unsafe because Claims of authority are easy to make and do not justify password disclosure. Option C is unsafe because Knowing a name is not independent identity verification. In practice: Refuse credential disclosure. End the interaction and confirm any legitimate request through a published contact channel. Key takeaway: Authority, familiarity and urgency are persuasion techniques—not proof of identity.
